stimuli.text: Researchers want to investigate whether a new fertilizer increases tomato yield. They have 40 garden plots available.

Random samples of 15 were taken from two groups. The values of reaction time (hundredths of a second) are:

**Morning:** 12, 13, 15, 18, 19, 19, 21, 25, 25, 25, 27, 27, 27, 27, 30

**Evening:** 14, 14, 16, 16, 19, 22, 24, 24, 24, 27, 29, 32, 43, 44, 73
A school district claims that 40% of its students take public transit to school. A reporter suspects the true proportion is higher. In a random sample of 360 students, 166 take public transit.

Data were collected on age of car (years) (x) and price (thousands of dollars) (y) for a sample of used cars. A scatterplot shows a linear pattern, and the residual plot shows no pattern. Computer output for the least-squares regression is shown.

```text
Predictor   Coef      SE Coef
Constant    51.9
x           -2.1
S = 4    R-Sq = 88.0%
```

questions.stem: Two independent random samples have n₁ = 17, s₁ = 4 and n₂ = 52, s₂ = 18. What is the standard error of x̄₁ − x̄₂?

options.why: Variances add, even for a difference.
Add variances, then take the square root; standard errors do not add.
Correct. √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).
Each sample contributes s²/n.

questions.stem: A principal divides students by grade level and takes a simple random sample of 25 students from each grade. What sampling method is this?

options.why: Cluster sampling selects whole groups.
The selection is random.
That selects every kth individual.
Correct. SRSs within groups (strata).

questions.stem: Why is the t distribution used instead of the normal distribution for inference about a mean?

options.text: Because σ is estimated by s, which adds variability
options.why: Correct. t has heavier tails to account for it.

options.text: Because the sample is always biased
options.why: Bias is unrelated.

options.text: Because sample means are never normal
options.why: They often are approximately normal.

options.text: Because t is used only for proportions
options.why: It is used for means.

questions.explanation: t has heavier tails to account for it.

questions.stem: The data are: 19, 25, 27, 30, 30, 35, 36, 38, 58. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, which statement is correct?

options.text: Q1 = 26, Q3 = 37; values above 53.5 are outliers, so 58 is an outlier
options.why: Correct. IQR = 11; upper fence = Q3 + 1.5·IQR = 53.5.

options.text: There are no outliers because every value is within 2 standard deviations of the mean
options.why: The 1.5 × IQR rule is the method asked for.

options.text: Q1 = 26, Q3 = 37; values above 46.5 are outliers
options.why: Add 1.5·IQR to Q3, not to the median.

options.text: Q1 = 26, Q3 = 37; values above 48 are outliers, so 58 is an outlier
options.why: The fence uses 1.5 × IQR, not 1 × IQR.

questions.stem: For a set of data, x̄ = 11, sx = 13, ȳ = 63, sy = 31 and r = 0.5. What is the least-squares regression line?

options.why: Multiply sy/sx by r.
a = ȳ − b·x̄.
The slope is r·sy/sx, not r·sx/sy.
Correct. b = r·sy/sx and a = ȳ − b·x̄.

questions.stem: P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A and B) = 0.2. What is P(A or B), and are A and B independent?

options.why: Compare P(A and B) with P(A)·P(B) = 0.2.
Subtract P(A and B) so the overlap is not counted twice.
Correct. P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); independent if P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.2.
P(A and B) is not 0, so they are not mutually exclusive.

questions.stem: A variable is approximately normal with mean 66 and standard deviation 4. What value is at the 75th percentile?

options.why: Use the z-score for the percentile, not the percentile itself.
Correct. z = invNorm(0.75) ≈ 0.674; x = μ + zσ.
Check the sign of z.
Multiply z by σ, not σ².

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for p is (0.42, 0.51). Which claim is supported?

options.text: Exactly 46.5% of the population has the trait
options.why: The center is an estimate.

options.text: There is a 95% probability that p is between 0.42 and 0.51
options.why: The probability statement applies to the method, not this interval.

options.text: It is plausible that fewer than half the population has the trait
options.why: Correct. Values below 0.5 lie in the interval.

options.text: The population proportion must be greater than 0.5
options.why: Most of the interval is below 0.5.

questions.explanation: Values below 0.5 lie in the interval.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for μ₁ − μ₂ is (−2.4, 5.1). What can be concluded?

options.text: There is no convincing evidence of a difference in population means, because 0 is in the interval
options.why: Correct. Zero is a plausible difference.
Negative differences are also plausible.
Positive differences are also plausible.

options.text: The two means are exactly equal
options.why: The interval does not prove equality.

questions.stem: For a distribution of time spent on homework, the mean is 36 and the median is 26. Which is the most likely shape?

options.why: Correct. A long right tail pulls the mean above the median.
A uniform distribution is symmetric, with mean near the median.
The mean is pulled toward the tail.
In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are close.

questions.explanation: Mean 36 > median 26: the mean is pulled toward the right tail.

questions.stem: A factory tests H₀: the defect rate is 2% versus Hₐ: it is greater than 2%. What is a Type I error in this context?

options.text: Concluding the defect rate is greater than 2% when it actually is 2%
options.why: Correct. Rejecting a true H₀.
That is a sampling problem.

options.text: Correctly finding that the rate is higher
options.why: That is a correct decision.

options.text: Concluding the defect rate is 2% when it is actually higher
options.why: That is a Type II error.

questions.stem: Which change increases the power of a significance test, with everything else unchanged?

options.text: Using a two-sided instead of a one-sided test
options.why: For the correct direction, that lowers power.
Correct. Larger samples detect real effects more often.
That lowers power.
That lowers power.

questions.explanation: Larger samples detect real effects more often.

questions.stem: What is the expected value of X?

options.why: That is the largest probability, not the mean.
Correct. μ = Σ x·P(x).
Weight each value by its probability.
That is the most likely value (mode), not the mean.

questions.stem: Each of 6 independent devices fails with probability 0.02. What is the probability that at least one fails?

options.why: Correct. 1 − P(none fail) = 1 − (1 − p)^n.
That is the probability all fail.
Probabilities of overlapping events cannot simply be added.
That is the probability none fail.

questions.stem: A test of H₀: p = 0.4 versus Hₐ: p > 0.4 gives a p-value of 0.03. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: There is a 0.97 probability that Hₐ is true
options.why: Not a valid interpretation.

options.text: There is a 0.03 probability that H₀ is true
options.why: A p-value is not the probability of a hypothesis.

options.text: If p = 0.4, there is a 0.03 probability of a sample proportion at least as large as the one observed, by chance alone
options.why: Correct. That is the definition of the p-value.
Unrelated to the p-value.

questions.explanation: That is the definition of the p-value.

questions.stem: What is the expected value of X?

options.why: That is the largest probability, not the mean.
Weight each value by its probability.
That is the most likely value (mode), not the mean.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 190 customers of an online store, 38 would recommend it to a friend. Which is a 99% confidence interval for the proportion of all customers of an online store who would recommend it to a friend?

options.why: Use the standard error, √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).
Divide by n inside the square root.
Use z* for 99%, not 1.96.
Correct. p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) with z* = 2.576.

questions.stem: Two independent random samples have n₁ = 31, s₁ = 14 and n₂ = 51, s₂ = 11. What is the standard error of x̄₁ − x̄₂?

options.why: Add variances, then take the square root; standard errors do not add.
Variances add, even for a difference.
Each sample contributes s²/n.
Correct. √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).

questions.stem: The correlation between temperature and ice cream sales is r = -0.7. Which is a correct interpretation of r²?

options.text: About 49% of the predictions are correct
options.why: r² is about variation explained, not accuracy of individual predictions.

options.text: Temperature causes 49% of ice cream sales
options.why: Regression does not establish causation.

options.text: About 49% of the variation in ice cream sales is accounted for by the linear model relating ice cream sales to temperature
options.why: Correct. r² is the proportion of variation in y explained by the linear model.

options.text: About 70% of the variation in ice cream sales is accounted for by the model
options.why: Square r.

questions.stem: A student is chosen at random from those who drive to school. What is the probability the student is a junior?

options.why: That is P(junior) overall.
Correct. P(junior | drives) = juniors who drive ÷ all who drive.
That is P(junior and drives); divide by drivers only.
That is P(drives | junior).

questions.stem: In an experiment on a new reading program, students are first grouped by reading level, then randomly assigned to programs within each level. What is the purpose of grouping by level?

options.text: Blocking, to reduce variability caused by reading level
options.why: Correct. Blocking controls a known source of variation.
That is a sampling idea.
Groups by level are not placebo groups.
It remains an experiment.

questions.explanation: Blocking controls a known source of variation.

options.text: Q1 = 18.5, Q3 = 39; values above 64.8 are outliers

options.text: Q1 = 18.5, Q3 = 39; values above 69.8 are outliers, so 77 is an outlier

options.why: It is quantitative.
Height and weight are positively related.
Unrelated.

options.text: Extrapolation beyond the range of the data
options.why: Correct. The pattern may not hold for adults.

questions.explanation: The pattern may not hold for adults.

questions.stem: Each of 20 students takes a reading test before and after a summer program. Which procedure compares the scores?

options.why: Scores are quantitative.

options.text: A paired t procedure on the differences (after − before)
options.why: Correct. Two measurements on the same students are paired.
That is for categorical data.
The samples are not independent.

questions.explanation: Two measurements on the same students are paired.

questions.stem: The regression line is ŷ = 35 − 1.5x. An observation has x = 5 and y = 32.6. What is its residual, and what does it mean?

options.text: 5.1; the actual value is above the predicted value
options.why: Correct. Residual = y − ŷ.

options.text: 5.1; the actual value is below the predicted value
options.why: A positive residual means the point is above the line.

options.text: -5.1; the actual value is below the predicted value
options.why: Residual = actual − predicted, not predicted − actual.
That is the predicted value ŷ.

questions.stem: A random sample of 20 gives x̄ = 157.4 and s = 16. Test H₀: μ = 166 versus Hₐ: μ < 166. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: Divide by the standard error s/√n.
The alternative is one-sided.
Correct. t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with df = n − 1.
Use the t distribution, not the normal.

questions.stem: To test H₀: p = 0.4 versus Hₐ: p < 0.4, a random sample of 210 gives p̂ = 0.36. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: The alternative is one-sided.
The test's standard deviation uses p₀, not p̂.
Correct. z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n); one-sided p-value.
Find the area in the direction of Hₐ.

questions.stem: For a distribution of time spent on homework, the mean is 68 and the median is 80. Which is the most likely shape?

questions.stem: Each of 15 independent trials succeeds with probability 0.2. What is the probability of exactly 7 successes?

options.why: Use p for successes, not 1 − p.
Include the binomial coefficient and the failures.
Correct. Use the binomial distribution with n = 15 and p = 0.2.
That is P(X ≤ k); the question asks for exactly k.

options.why: Divide s by √n.
Divide by √n, not n.
With s estimating σ, use t*, not z*.

options.why: Correct. Means add or subtract; variances add.

questions.stem: What is the smallest sample size needed to estimate a proportion with a margin of error of at most 0.04 at 95% confidence, with no prior estimate of p?

options.why: Always round up to guarantee the margin.

Square z*/m.

questions.stem: In a randomized experiment, 70 of 260 subjects improved with treatment 1 and 28 of 90 improved with treatment 2. For a test of H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0, what is the test statistic?

options.why: Correct. Pooled p̂c = 0.28; z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂)/√(p̂c(1 − p̂c)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)).
Use (1/n₁ + 1/n₂).
The test uses the pooled proportion, because H₀ assumes p₁ = p₂.
Divide the difference by its standard error.

questions.stem: In a randomized experiment, 109 of 210 subjects improved with treatment 1 and 38 of 150 improved with treatment 2. For a test of H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0, what is the test statistic?

options.why: Divide the difference by its standard error.
Correct. Pooled p̂c = 0.4083; z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂)/√(p̂c(1 − p̂c)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)).
The test uses the pooled proportion, because H₀ assumes p₁ = p₂.
Use (1/n₁ + 1/n₂).

questions.stem: For a chi-square test of homogeneity on these counts, what are the test statistic and degrees of freedom?

options.why: For a two-way table, df = (r − 1)(c − 1).
Correct. χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E with df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1).
Do not divide by the total.
Do not take a square root.

questions.stem: In a randomized experiment, 80 of 200 subjects improved with treatment 1 and 154 of 280 improved with treatment 2. For a test of H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0, what is the test statistic?

parts.prompt: Write an investigative question for this study, and identify the explanatory and response variables.

rubric.criterion: A clear investigative question that names the population or units and the variables.
rubric.example: "Does the new fertilizer lead to a better total weight of tomatoes harvested than the standard fertilizer for units like these?"
Explanatory: treatment (the new fertilizer vs the standard fertilizer). Response: total weight of tomatoes harvested.

parts.prompt: Explain why an experiment, rather than an observational study, should be used to answer the question.

rubric.criterion: Only random assignment allows a cause-and-effect conclusion; an observational study could be confounded.
rubric.example: Units that choose a treatment may differ in other ways that affect the response.

parts.prompt: Describe how to randomly assign the 40 units to the two treatments in a completely randomized design.

rubric.example: Number units 1–40; use a random number generator to select 20 different numbers.
Those 20 receive the new fertilizer; the remaining 20 receive the standard fertilizer.

parts.prompt: The researchers consider blocking by sun exposure (full sun or partial shade). Explain how blocking would be carried out and why it could improve the experiment.

rubric.criterion: Form blocks and randomize within each block.
rubric.example: Separate units into the blocks, then randomly assign half of each block to each treatment.

rubric.criterion: Benefit: reduces variability in the response due to the blocking variable, making a treatment effect easier to detect.
rubric.example: Accounts for differences caused by sun exposure.

parts.prompt: Compare the distributions of the two groups (shape, center and variability) in context.

Evening is more variable (IQR 16 vs 9).

rubric.criterion: Comments on shape or unusual features.
rubric.example: Evening has a high outlier, suggesting right skew.

parts.prompt: Which measure of center is more appropriate for Evening, the mean or the median? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Median, because it is resistant to the outlier or skew.
rubric.example: Mean 28.1 is pulled toward the high value; median 24 is not.

parts.prompt: State the hypotheses, defining the parameter.

rubric.criterion: Correct hypotheses with the parameter defined.
rubric.example: H₀: p = 0.4; Hₐ: p > 0.4, where p is the proportion of all district students who take public transit.

parts.prompt: Identify the appropriate procedure and check its conditions.

rubric.criterion: One-sample z test for a proportion.
rubric.example: Random sample stated.
360 is less than 10% of all students (assumed); np₀ = 144 and n(1 − p₀) = 216 are both at least 10.

parts.prompt: Calculate the test statistic and p-value.
State a conclusion in context at α = 0.05.

rubric.criterion: Correct decision linked to the p-value, in context.
rubric.example: Because 0.009 is less than 0.05, reject H₀: convincing evidence that the proportion is greater than 0.4.

parts.prompt: Write the equation of the least-squares regression line, defining the variables.

rubric.example: ŷ = 51.9 − 2.1x, where ŷ is predicted price (thousands of dollars) and x is age of car (years).

parts.prompt: Interpret the slope and the value of R-Sq in context.

rubric.example: For each additional unit of age of car (years), the predicted price (thousands of dollars) decreases by about 2.1.
About 88.0% of the variation in price (thousands of dollars) is accounted for by the linear model with age of car (years).

parts.prompt: One observation has x = 5 and y = 43.2. Calculate and interpret its residual. Also find the correlation r.

rubric.example: ŷ = 41.4; residual = 43.2 − 41.4 = 1.8: the actual value is above the prediction.

parts.prompt: The data come from a convenience sample. Explain how this affects the conclusions and describe a better data collection method.

rubric.criterion: Results may not generalize to the population; a random sample would allow generalization.
rubric.example: Take a simple random sample of used cars from the population of interest. Observational data also cannot show causation.
